extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians and philosophers of mathematics (graduate students and researchers) interested in foundations, constructivism, and applications to physics
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for assessing the philosophical and mathematical legitimacy, applicability, and meaning of constructivist/intuitionist vs classical mathematics, especially regarding proofs, existence claims, and applications to physical sciences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intuitionism as a legitimate foundational framework
rubrics_metrics.description: "Intuitionism should be studied as part of mathematics." (Heyting) — intuitionism is one possible foundational framework among others and has 'the good right' to coexist with classical mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat intuitionism not as claiming a monopoly but as a legitimate alternative standpoint. Compare removing LEM to eliminating a classical axiom (e.g., Pappus in projective geometry); acknowledge both its intrinsic intellectual value and its limited direct applications, while allowing mutual study and cross-fertilization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerical meaning (Bishop's notion of meaning)
rubrics_metrics.description: Meaning should be tied to 'the relation of the results to the real world' and to a notion of numerical or cognitive significance rather than abstract truth alone (Bishop).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate mathematical propositions by their numerical/cognitive significance and relevance to empirical sciences. Bishop argues this notion should precede notions of truth and rigor; use this standard when judging the practical or explanatory value of mathematical work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive validity / requirement of constructive proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructive existence assertions require the ability to find (compute) witnesses; under Heyting semantics an existence proof amounts to exhibiting a computable function that identifies the witness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether existence claims supply an explicit method or algorithm to produce the object. Indirect proofs by contradiction that only assert existence without a method are not constructively acceptable. Use computability/constructibility as a key test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feasibility of Bishop's 'sifting' (translating classical to constructive)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bishop's program proposes translating absolute classical statements into relative/constructive assertions (e.g., 'LPO → A') as a comprehensive sift of classical material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge attempts to 'constructivize' classical results by whether a faithful, informative translation exists; be alert to objections (McCarthy) that not all classical statements are capturable, and to ambiguities (e.g., due to Gödel incompleteness) about what is intended by such translations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applications to physics as a relevance/litmus test
rubrics_metrics.description: Some (e.g., Bishop, Weyl by citation) view the applicability of mathematics to physics as central to its justification; others (Dummett) reject empirical application as relevant to philosophical foundations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating foundational frameworks, consider whether they support the mathematics used in physics and other sciences. Debate exists: positive appraisal if a framework preserves scientific applicability; critique if framework prioritizes philosophical purity over empirical utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of non-standard analysis and the transfer principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Robinson's non-standard analysis gives precise sense to infinitesimals and, via the transfer principle, extends first-order real statements to the hyperreals; Heyting praised Robinson's work for connecting abstract model theory to elementary calculus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess frameworks by whether they render historically or heuristically useful notions (e.g., infinitesimals, Dirac's δ) mathematically precise and whether they enable concrete applications in applied mathematics, physics, economics, or pedagogy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependence of variational existence results on LEM (extreme value theorem)
rubrics_metrics.description: Calculus of variations and many existence results (e.g., geodesics, minimal surfaces, Plateau's problem) rely on the extreme value theorem, which is not available without the law of excluded middle (LEM).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether variational theorems and global existence results can be recast constructively; recognize that many such results resist constructivization, and that loss of these classical theorems may impair applicability to physics and geometry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problematic nature of indirect (proof-by-contradiction) arguments for constructivists
rubrics_metrics.description: Many classical proofs (e.g., the Hawking–Penrose theorem) use indirect proofs. Such proofs assert existence by contradiction rather than by constructing witnesses, challenging constructive validation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging a theorem's constructive status, analyze proof methods: indirect proofs may preclude constructivist acceptance even if the classical statement has empirical significance. Strive to find direct or constructive alternatives, or else classify the result as non-constructively established.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geodesic incompleteness as the working criterion for 'singularity'
rubrics_metrics.description: In general relativity the Hawking–Penrose theorem is best understood as asserting geodesic incompleteness (past-endless geodesics of finite length) rather than a 'place' singularity; careful definition matters (Wald).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use geodesic incompleteness, not intuitive 'endpoints' or 'places', as the mathematical criterion for singularities. Avoid conflating heuristic physical language with precise geometric statements; such conflation led to errors in secondary literature (Billinge).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutual enrichment: coexistence of classical and intuitionistic mathematics (numerical constructivism)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is scope for reconciliation: Heyting and others recognize that classical and intuitionistic subjects can be intertwined; numerical constructivism aims to preserve post-LEM numerical meaning while respecting constructive standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate frameworks by their capacity to coexist and inform one another (e.g., recognizing concrete, post-LEM meaningful applications within a broader constructive outlook). Favor approaches that allow bridging rather than absolutist rejection of the other side.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequacy of constructivist frameworks for empirical refutation and scientific practice (Tennant's claim)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tennant claims a constructivist version of a theory can be adequate for all applications in natural science and that underlying logic can be taken very weak; critics argue these claims lack substantiation, especially regarding confirmation and probabilification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess claims that constructive logics suffice for scientific practice by examining whether they accommodate confirmation, probabilistic reasoning, and the specific mathematical tools used in sciences; be cautious about overbroad claims without demonstrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algorithmic decidability implications of Heyting semantics
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Heyting semantics, certain classical proofs translate into claims that predicates are effectively decidable (Shapiro's example), which may be an implausible consequence for intuitionistic semantics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When translating classical proofs into constructive/Heyting semantics, check for unintended strong algorithmic consequences (e.g., implying decidability of arbitrary predicates). Such consequences can indicate a mismatch between semantic interpretation and intended constructive standards.
